History & Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
32-year-old patient with chronic atopic eczema presents via video with a 4–5-day worsening flare of diffuse, intensely pruritic, dry erythematous rash; plan for stronger topical steroid (Betnovate) and oral antihistamine (fexofenadine) instituted.

History:
• Presenting complaint: “Sore, red, very itchy, dry skin” over chest, hands, arms—worst in antecubital fossae.  
• Onset/progression: Began “past few days,” rapidly worsening; more severe than prior flares.  
• Character: Diffuse erythema and dryness with cracks; no weeping/exudate; no lichenification reported.  
• Aggravating factors: Scratching increases itch.  
• Relieving factors: None identified; current emollients and OTC hydrocortisone not helping.  
• Associated symptoms: Denies fever, joint pain, breathing difficulty.  
• Review of systems (pertinent negatives): No systemic symptoms, no known triggers/environmental change mentioned.

Past Medical History:
• Atopic dermatitis (eczema) – chronic, usually managed with emollients and OTC hydrocortisone.  
• Asthma – mild/intermittent; uses short-acting bronchodilator PRN, no current respiratory issues.

Medications:
• Diprobase cream (emollient) – topical, dose/route/frequency not documented (patient states “every day”).  
• Dermol wash – topical cleanser, dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Hydrocortisone cream (OTC, 1% presumed) – topical, “not helping.”  
• Salbutamol “blue” inhaler – inhaled PRN, dose/frequency not documented.  
• Previously tried cetirizine (OTC antihistamine) – ineffective.  
Allergies: “No known drug allergies.”

Social History:
• Residence: London, secure environment for video consult.  
• Tobacco, alcohol, recreational drugs: Not discussed (not recorded).  
• Occupation/other: Not discussed.

Family History:
• Mother – hypothyroidism and migraine (clinician later repeated “hyperthyroidism” – conflict noted).  
• No other familial conditions mentioned.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded (video consult).  
• General/skin (visual): Widespread erythematous, dry patches over chest, arms, hands; most pronounced in antecubital folds. Visible skin cracking; no weeping, exudate, lichenification, or scratch marks reported.  
• Other systems: Not examined.

Investigations:
• None performed or ordered during visit.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Likely acute flare of chronic atopic dermatitis (eczema) with inadequate response to current low-potency steroid and emollients.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Atopic dermatitis flare – chronic history, classic flexural involvement, pruritus; no systemic signs.  
2. Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis – possible given sudden worsening, but patient denies product changes.  
3. Scabies infestation – intense itch and flexural sites could fit, but absent burrows, nocturnal itch, or contact history.

Issue 1 – Atopic dermatitis flare
Assessment: Significant, widespread flare refractory to OTC hydrocortisone and emollients.  
Plan:  
• Topical steroid: Betnovate (betamethasone valerate 0.1%) cream thinly (≈ fingertip unit) to affected areas BID x 14 days; counsel on fingertip-unit dosing.  
• Oral antihistamine: Fexofenadine 180 mg PO daily (dose per standard; actual dose not stated—prescription sent).  
• Continue regular emollients (Diprobase, Dermol) liberally and avoid potential irritants.  
• Safety-net: Return sooner if rash worsens, becomes painful, weepy, or signs of infection/allergy develop.  
• Follow-up: Re-evaluate in 2 weeks or earlier if needed.

Issue 2 – Asthma (stable)
Assessment: Intermittent; currently asymptomatic.  
Plan: Continue PRN salbutamol inhaler; no change required today.

General plan items:
• Prescription sent electronically to patient’s nominated Boots pharmacy.  
• Educated on proper steroid application, avoidance of overuse, and ongoing skin hydration.  
• Advised to monitor for side effects (skin thinning, allergic reaction) and to seek care if uncontrolled.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: No vitals obtained; smoking/alcohol history not elicited; detailed medication doses/frequencies largely absent.  
• Transcript conflict: Patient reported mother with hypothyroidism; clinician later stated “hyperthyroidism” – conflict noted.  
• Transcript quality: Audio clear; occasional incomplete sentences but core clinical info intact.
